title: Population Assessment of Sperm Whales in the Mascarene Region (Western Indian Ocean): Emerging Signs of Decline and Conservation Perspectives
content:
ABSTRACT

Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) are predominantly oceanic cetaceans exhibiting marked habitat diversity, ranging from nomadic populations to resident units associated with small oceanic islands. Understanding spatial structure and population parameters at a regional scale is essential for effective conservation and management. The Mascarene region represents a critical yet understudied sperm whale habitat in the Western Indian Ocean. This study provides the first population assessment of sperm whales in the Mascarene region and of the resident subpopulation off Mauritius. A mark–recapture approach based on photo-identification was applied over a 17-year period (2008–2024). Results demonstrate the presence of female and immature sperm whale groups representing all three habitat specializations: nomadic, regional residents, and island specialists. The Mascarene population is estimated at approximately 144 individuals, including an average of 26 resident sperm whales off Mauritius. However, analyses reveal increased mortality in the 2020s, threatening regional population viability. Moreover, the resident subpopulation shows instability in age structure, with a decline in adult females that may lead to its collapse. Given the global rarity of this island-associated ecotype, these trends may have significant ecological and socioeconomic implications, underscoring the need for urgent, targeted conservation measures in the region.
